title: Hubble’s Distant View of the Supernova Remnant 1E 0102.2-7219 in 2006
caption: The supernova remnant 1E 0102.2-7219 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Just below the center of this picture sits a greenish-blue shell of debris, the remains of an exploded star. It is the supernova remnant E0102, in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy near the Milky Way. In the upper right glows its neighbor N 76, a star-forming region in lavender and peach tones.

The two look different because they are made of different stuff. N 76 shines mainly with hydrogen, while E0102 is rich in oxygen and has almost no hydrogen or helium. One idea is that the star that exploded had blown away its outer hydrogen in a strong wind first. It may have been a Wolf-Rayet star.
At only about 2000 years old, E0102 is young. That lets astronomers study material from a massive star's core directly, learning how stars are built and how they enrich their surroundings.
scale: The Small Magellanic Cloud lies roughly 210,000 light-years away, according to the caption.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the region in 2003 through blue, visible, infrared and hydrogen filters, combined with oxygen-emission images from Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Filters that isolate the glow of particular gases, such as oxygen and hydrogen, bring out color differences an eye would not see.

explore: E0102 lies almost 50 light-years from the edge of N 76. Wolf-Rayet stars can be upward of 20 times the Sun's mass and tens of thousands of times as luminous, and they have strong winds throughout their lives.
